text:
The UK will not have to follow the EU and apply tariffs on Chinese car imports under an Irish proposal that could prove another breakthrough for Andy Burnham in his reset of relations with the bloc.
Ireland, which holds the rotating EU presidency and plays a chief role in progressing legislation, has come up with a compromise under which the UK would be included in the bloc’s new “Made in Europe” legislation without having to align with the EU’s trade policies.
Made in Europe, or the Industrial Acceleration Act (IAA), is designed to protect the bloc’s supply chains from cheap competition, mainly from China and mainly in the automotive and clean energy sectors.
It is understood that in a fourth compromise text, due to be considered by EU competition ministers on 3 December, Ireland has proposed giving the European Economic Area, Switzerland and the UK “partner” status when it comes to the assembly of cars.
This would allow not only cars such as the Mini, made at BMW’s Oxford factory, to qualify as European, but also vehicles made by the Japanese firm Nissan at its vast Sunderland plant.
As part of the compromise, a “partner” country would agree to mutual access to whatever subsidies are available to EU-owned assembly plants and public procurement contracts when it comes to fleet cars.
As part of the proposal, Irish negotiators have also suggested allowing Japan and South Korea, which lobbied hard against the original Made in Europe proposals, to have access to public procurement and other public support schemes when it comes to car parts and components.
A spokesperson for the Irish presidency said: “Having listened closely to all member states, the presidency has proposed a pragmatic and balanced way forward on the IAA to deliver for European competitiveness.”
Andy Burnham last week took the biggest step towards deeper ties with the EU since Brexit, sealing deals to ease trade and create a mobility scheme for young people.
The latest iteration of the IAA text is designed to reflect the car sector’s position as a cornerstone of European industry.
France, which devised the legislation, originally opposed the inclusion of the UK at all but dropped its opposition last month on condition that the UK dynamically align with the EU on tariffs on Chinese vehicles.
But this caused further tensions with the UK. The business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, insisted the British government would not be coerced into imposing tariffs on Chinese vehicles and would only take steps that were in the national interest.
Mike Hawes, the chief executive of the Society of Motor Manufacturers, said the UK “should not become collateral damage” from measures intended to address concerns arising elsewhere in the global market.
The UK car industry has argued that it is so intertwined with its EU counterparts that both sides would be damaged if the UK was not included in Made in Europe.
Hawes said: “It is essential that the final arrangements recognise the unique UK-EU automotive relationship as allies in adversity, and do not create new barriers to our shared supply chains.”
The latest proposal will be discussed by an EU working group involving industry leaders and EU member states on Friday, before being finessed further for consideration by ministers.
European carmakers are attempting to respond to a flood of cheap Chinese electric vehicles into the bloc. Volkswagen began wage talks with labour representatives on Tuesday amid mounting worker anger over deep cost cuts, with protesters carrying black coffins to symbolise what they said was the death of trust and the company’s future prospects.
China is squaring up to the increased prospect of being partially restricted in trade with the EU, with tariffs imposed on Chinese EV imports in 2024, and quotas agreed with Beijing in October coming into force on 1 December.
The Chinese electric vehicle maker BYD said on Tuesday that it has entered into exclusive negotiations with the billionaire Jim Ratcliffe’s Ineos Automotive to buy its manufacturing plant in ‌Hambach, France, ‌as it seeks ‌more European production ahead of Made in Europe legislation next year.
Separately, Ineos said on Tuesday it would begin production of its Grenadier 4x4 in the US in 2028.
